sentences.text: Nanotyrannus was a mid-sized tyrannosauroid, a type of large theropod dinosaur.
Unlike the massive skulls of adult tyrannosaurs, this species had a slender, low skull with small crests in front of its eyes and smooth, chisel-shaped teeth that lacked serrations.
The holotype skull, which is the specimen the species is based on, measures 57.2 centimeters from the front tip of the premaxilla to the back tip of the quadrate bone.
Teeth from multiple individuals of this species have been found embedded in the bones of herbivores.
Large muscle attachment sites at the rear of the skull suggest the animal could flex its head side to side with great strength.

The species N. lancensis was first described in 1946 by Charles W. Gilmore as a new species of Gorgosaurus, but the type specimen is actually skull CMNH 7541, collected in 1942 by David Hosbrook Dunkle.
The genus Nanotyrannus was later named by Bakker and colleagues in 1988 to separate this animal from Gorgosaurus.
Researchers suggest that the extremely long hind limbs indicate a lifestyle adapted for pursuit predation, differing from the ambush style of larger tyrannosaurids.
A 2021 study estimated the bite force of juvenile tyrannosaurs, including the specimen known as Jane, to be between 5,269 and 5,641 Newtons, which is higher than previous estimates.
Bakker suggests that due to its weight and build, Nanotyrannus hunted in packs.
A 2026 study based on bone histology found that the growth trajectories of Nanotyrannus specimens did not fit the growth curve model of adult T. rex, suggesting a distinct subadult stage.

Nanotyrannus morphology combines traits from basal tyrannosauroids like Moros and Xiongguanlong with those of derived tyrannosaurids, leading recent studies to classify it as a member of the clade Nanotyrannidae.
The type species of the genus Nanotyrannus is Nanotyrannus lancensis.
Nanotyrannus fossils date to the Late Maastrichtian age, living in western North America approximately 67 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous.
The environment was warm, humid, and swampy with maritime to subtropical conditions.
Fossils of Nanotyrannid teeth, potentially belonging to Nanotyrannus, have been found in the Lance Formation.

Many researchers believe the original Nanotyrannus skull belongs to an immature Tyrannosaurus rex rather than a distinct species, arguing that the difference in tooth count between 15-16 and 11-12 is simply a sign of growth. Some scientists argue that Nanotyrannus is distinct because of these tooth counts, while others note that the lack of serrations might be a sign of juvenile development or a unique diagnostic trait. Researchers concluded that the N. lancensis holotype belongs to a mature individual and is therefore a species distinct from Tyrannosaurus rex, and some paleontologists who previously doubted Nanotyrannus accepted it as a valid taxon after Zanno and Napoli's paper, specifically agreeing the Bloody Mary specimen is distinct. It is debated whether the lack of serrations on Nanotyrannus teeth is a sign of juvenile development or a unique diagnostic trait of the species, and researchers note that further testing and more data are required to determine which phylogenetic analysis of Nanotyrannus relationships is correct.
